title: Is the problem real?
principle: A bad fix people already use proves the pain is real.

screens.text: Let me start in Bengaluru, around 2005. A young man named P.C. Musthafa often visited his cousin's grocery shop. The shop sold idli-dosa batter from a local maker, in a plain plastic bag tied with a rubber band. It had no brand and no maker's name.

screens.prompt: Buyers complained about that batter: the messy bags, the quality and the cleanliness. What do you think happened to sales?

options.label: They fell. People stopped buying it
They stayed the same. People kept buying
Only a few regular buyers stayed

screens.why: They stayed the same. One report says there were complaints, but sales didn't fall. People didn't like the bag, but they still wanted ready batter.

screens.title: The clue in the bag
screens.text: Musthafa saw a clue. People complained about the bags, but they kept paying for them. In 2006, he and four cousins started iD, their own batter brand, in a tiny room next to the shop. By 2015, iD sold about ₹100 crore a year.

screens.title: The workaround test
screens.text: A workaround is a bad fix people use because nothing better exists. Y Combinator, a well-known startup school in America, calls the worst pain a "hair on fire" problem: with your hair on fire, you'd use any fix, even a bad one. A bad fix people pay for proves pain.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: iD grew into a ₹100 crore company, but the same clue works in a colony. Imagine you want to start a food business from home. Your colony has about 100 families. You have ₹40,000 saved and three ideas, but you can try only one.

screens.prompt: Which of your three ideas has the strongest proof that people need it?

options.label: Eggless cakes. Mothers take an auto 6 km to get them
Fusion cakes. 40 friends at your party told you to start
Office lunches. An app says tiffin orders are rising in your city

screens.why: Yes. The mothers already spend time and auto fare on a bad fix. That trouble, in your own colony, is your proof.

wrong.b: Your friends lose nothing by telling you to start. Nobody is going to any trouble for fusion cakes yet.
wrong.c: Growth across a city tells you nothing about your street. Nobody near you is doing anything to get office lunches yet.

screens.prompt: Say 30 families buy 4 eggless cakes a year, each needing a ₹120 auto trip. You deliver for ₹40, same cake price. Families' yearly saving?
screens.why: Right. 30 × 4 = 120 cakes. Each saves ₹120 − ₹40 = ₹80, and 120 × ₹80 = ₹9,600 a year. That is what your service saves them, in rupees.

wrong.a: That is what they spend on autos now: 120 trips × ₹120. But they still pay you ₹40 a cake, so each saves ₹80: 120 × ₹80 = ₹9,600.
wrong.c: That's 120 × ₹40, what they pay you for delivery. The saving is ₹120 − ₹40 = ₹80 a cake: 120 × ₹80 = ₹9,600.

screens.title: When nobody has a fix
screens.text: Sometimes nobody has a fix because none exists yet. That can still be a great problem if people keep looking for a fix again and again. But if there is no fix and nobody looks for one, the pain is probably small. Check before you spend.

screens.prompt: Here are three problems in your colony. Which one should you check first?

options.label: Late-night snacks. No shop is open after 11
Tailoring. Two tailors nearby, both busy
Pet care. Owners keep posting "Who can feed my cat?"

screens.why: Yes. Nobody offers pet care, but owners keep looking for help. That shows a real need, even when no fix exists yet.

wrong.a: No shop is open, but has anyone asked for late-night snacks or looked for them? Nothing shows that. The pet owners keep looking for help.
wrong.b: Busy tailors mean people already have a fix that works. The pet owners keep looking for help but find none.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six things you may notice. For each one, tell me: are people already going to trouble because of it?

items.text: Parents pay a cousin ₹200 a week to bring tiffin from a cook 3 km away
Friends say they'd love a gym in the colony
Shopkeepers write udhaar in a notebook, but still lose money when they forget who owes them
Office workers queue 20 minutes every morning at the only breakfast cart nearby
In a survey, most people say they'd try a new snack

screens.why: Paying a cousin, using a notebook but still losing money, and waiting in a 20-minute queue are bad fixes people already use. Likes, surveys and "I'd love it" cost nothing, so they prove nothing yet.

screens.setup: You pick eggless cakes. A bakery 6 km away charges ₹700 for a 1 kg cake. You'll charge ₹700 too, plus ₹40 for delivery, which pays for petrol. Each cake costs you ₹350 to make. You have ₹40,000 saved. A neighbour says, "A shop on the main road, at ₹15,000 a month, would bring walk-in buyers from the whole area."
screens.question: How do you start?

options.label: Rent the shop for walk-in buyers from the whole area
options.outcome: You rent the shop. In the first month, you sell 20 cakes and make ₹7,000. The rent is ₹15,000, so you lose ₹8,000. At that rate, your ₹40,000 lasts five months.
options.why: The shop brought 20 orders in a month, but not ₹15,000 more profit. And the mothers' problem was the 6 km trip, not that there was no shop nearby.
options.better: Bake at home and deliver to the colony mothers first.

options.label: Put up posters all over the area, then start
options.outcome: The posters cost ₹3,000 and bring 2 orders from new people, which leave you ₹700. The mothers who already make the 6 km trip have not heard from you yet.
options.why: Posters reach everyone, but you already knew your strongest buyers: the mothers making the 6 km trip.
options.better: Start with the mothers who already take an auto 6 km for these cakes.

options.label: Bake at home and deliver in the colony first
options.outcome: You keep your ₹40,000 safe and plan to bake at home. Before you bake even one cake for sale, you'll talk to the colony mothers who make the trip.
options.why: You went straight to people who already go to trouble for these cakes, and kept your costs tiny. That is where your first orders can come from.

screens.text: Words alone cost ___. A bad fix that people still ___ for proves the pain.
screens.why: Right. Likes and "I'd love it" cost nothing. The shop's buyers kept paying for messy bags, and your colony mothers pay for autos. That is the proof.

summary: Workaround: a clumsy fix people use because nothing better exists.
If people already pay or go to trouble for a bad fix, the pain is real.
If nobody uses any fix, ask why before you spend.

cards.front: Which is better proof that people want home tiffin?
options: Families pay ₹200 a week to fetch tiffin from far away
cards.back: Paying ₹200 a week is a workaround. Likes cost nothing.

cards.front: Nobody in your area does anything about a problem. What should you ask first?
options: Does it hurt enough to bother?
cards.back: No fix and no complaints often means the pain is small. Check before you spend.

cards.front: 20 families each make 5 trips a year, at ₹100 a trip. What do they spend on trips?
